Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

vignette: Eleanor Vance had spent her life navigating the tightrope between public duty and private dread. At eight years old, she had watched her mother’s partner shatter a ceramic vase against the hallway wall during a furious outburst. The crash of glass, the sharp scent of spilled whiskey, and her mother’s choked pleas were etched into her mind with painful precision. Other moments from those evenings simply vanished, swallowed by a fog she could not pierce no matter how hard she tried. When the trauma returned, it did not arrive as a narrative. Her body would instantly lock into the exact posture she had held that night—knees drawn to her chest, spine pressed flat against the peeling wallpaper, breath held tight against her ribs. She had come to believe that her own stillness was the only thing that kept her invisible, a survival tactic that never truly expired. Now thirty-nine, the city council chambers had become the stage where that old survival script played out in real time. During late committee sessions, a constituent’s narrowed eyes would instantly pull a fractured memory forward. The partial clarity of the childhood violence would flash behind her eyelids, and this intrusion did not merely recall the past; it directly triggered the threat. Her heart would hammer against her ribs, her muscles would coil, and the hallway wall would feel as close and real as the polished oak dais before her. She found herself tracking every face in the chamber, scanning for the micro-expressions of aggression she had learned to fear. When she detected a tightened jaw or a raised voice echoing from the gallery, the dread would spike, and she would physically withdraw, retreating into silence until the moment passed. Her nervous system never distinguished between a heated budget debate and the violent swings of her childhood. This constant vigilance, in turn, kept the traumatic fragments alive. Lying awake in her marital bedroom, Eleanor would watch her husband’s chest rise and fall, listening for any hitch that might signal irritation. Her eyes would track the shadows in the room, searching for sudden movements that could mimic the father’s approach. The very act of monitoring for hostility meant her brain never fully rested, and the unresolved gaps in her timeline kept cycling back. What frightened her most was that her own threat monitoring guaranteed the memories would resurface. She had started restricting her safe spaces to a handful of rooms in her home, unable to tolerate open doorways or crowded corridors. Over months, these habits had cost her; she missed town halls, snapped at colleagues who spoke too sharply, and grew distant from her husband as she retreated behind closed doors. Her sleep fractured into shallow, watchful intervals, leaving her exhausted and perpetually braced. The loop tightened until it became unsustainable. It was a recent zoning debate, where a colleague’s abrupt hand gesture left her physically paralyzed and unable to speak, that finally pushed her through the clinic’s doors. She feared she would lose her seat, but more than that, she was terrified of her own body betraying her again. She hoped to finally break the cycle, to stop her nervous system from translating ordinary tension into past terror, and to sit in the chamber without bracing for a blow that had already ended decades ago.
